title: Communicating Uncertainty Can Increase AI Adoption
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University - David A. Tepper School of Business, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and University of Toronto

detail.title: Communicating Uncertainty Can Increase AI Adoption
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) recommendations are inherently uncertain; however, many user interfaces do not communicate this. We document that communicating underlying uncertainty can increase adherence to AI recommendations. We conduct a randomized controlled experiment in which participants set prices for their short-term rental listings while being exposed to AI-recommended prices with or without explicit communication of uncertainty. Absent an AI recommendation or uncertainty information, participants typically select prices similar to the average competitor price. With AI recommendations, participants decrease their reliance on the average competitor price and appear to incorporate the AI recommendations into their prices. Communicating two distinct types of uncertainty leads to more adherence to AI recommendations and improved decision making, whether it is fundamental uncertainty (defined as the predicted booking probability at the AI-recommended price) or model uncertainty (defined as a confidence range around the AI-recommended price). We also find that providing feedback on booking outcomes increases adherence to the AI recommendation. Adding uncertainty information to the feedback further increases adherence. These results suggest that communicating uncertainty may improve adherence to AI recommendations, particularly when feedback is costly or inefficient.

title: From Notes to Bots: How Generative AI Impacts Human-Led Fact-Checking
affiliations: Georgia State University - Department of Computer Information Systems and

detail.title: From Notes to Bots: How Generative AI Impacts Human-Led Fact-Checking
detail.abstract: Human-led approaches, such as crowdsourced fact-checking, have been central to combating misinformation, but generative AI (GenAI) has recently emerged as an alternative, offering faster fact-check-like outputs. We examine how GenAI affects human-led fact-checking in the context of Grok (a GenAI chatbot) and Community Notes (X's crowdsourced fact-checking system). Leveraging the rollout of Grok's reply function, which enabled users to summon AI-generated fact-check-like replies, we find that its availability reduced user participation in Community Notes on both the demand and supply sides. Additionally, this disengagement effect is more pronounced for highly active contributors who are critical to the sustainability of Community Notes. This study enhances the understanding of the interdependence between fact-checking approaches.

This essay sought to pinpoint the major contributing variables and their impact on the digital divide. We gathered 185 samples for this study from various regions in Bangladesh's northern area. Policymakers and sociologists would benefit from this study's understanding of the causes of the digital divide, which should make it possible to close it in developing nations like Bangladesh.

detail.title: EHR-QC 2.0: LLM-driven medical concept mapping, FHIR support, and web-based interface
detail.abstract: \textbf{Background:}Our previous work introduced the open-source EHR-QC pipeline. This pipeline implements extraction, transform and load (ETL), pre-processing and quality control for biomedical and linked genomic information. These operations are necessary to make Electronic Health Record (EHR) data suitable for machine learning to model clinical outcomes. The original EHR-QC was developed to address a lack of open-source tools that enable these operations across vendors. Whilst effective, the EHR-QC tool had scope for development and requirements to update functionality to keep up with best practices, and extend its usage to a wider audience.  \textbf{Objectives:}This paper introduces EHR-QC 2.0, which represents a significant update to the original release. It aims to address the following issues:1) The biomedical terminology standardisation module uses multiple text similarity based algorithms to obtain matching ontology terms.2) The standardisation module is limited to the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership - Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) schema. This offers great data persistence and aggregation capabilities, but limited support for interoperability.3) The accessibility of the command-line interface and the reliance on static visualisations limit the full usability of the EHR-QC pipeline to a broad audience. \textbf{Methods:}The EHR-QC 2.0 presents an innovative update by leveraging an ensemble of large language models (LLMs) to perform robust semantic mapping. In this release, we extend support to the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) framework - an implementation of the Health Level 7 (HL7) data interoperability standard. Lastly, we developed a simple web platform that allows users to generate and explore dynamic visualisations directly through a web based graphical user interface, without needing to execute repetitive command-line operations. \textbf{Results:}This work documents the considerations and validation steps informing the implementation of the proposed updates. These updates enhance EHR-QC by enabling full automation, updating the tooling, improving data-exchange mechanisms, and expanding the platform’s target user base and usability. \textbf{Conclusions}With the release of EHR-QC 2.0 we have continued to provide open-source tools to support interoperability and data wrangling tools for cutting edge ML and AI tool development. This advancement is expected to support more effective resource allocation, promote the development of proactive and evidence-based treatment strategies, thus contributing to the reduction of overall healthcare expenditures.

title: Show Me the Tax: Identifying the Impact of Tax-Deductible Labeling on Charitable Crowdfunding
affiliations: Tulane University - A.B. Freeman School of Business, University of Waterloo, California State University, Long Beach - College of Business Administration and University of Oklahoma

detail.title: Show Me the Tax: Identifying the Impact of Tax-Deductible Labeling on Charitable Crowdfunding
detail.abstract: Charitable crowdfunding platforms have recently begun labeling eligible campaigns as "tax-deductible" to spotlight potential tax benefits for donors. Traditional economic and institutional legitimacy theories predict that emphasizing additional tax incentives will reduce perceived net donation costs and enhance perceived legitimacy, ultimately boosting donations. However, psychological perspectives warn that highlighting tax considerations may undermine donors' intrinsic motivations, shift focus away from emotional engagement, or trigger anxiety over complex tax filing requirements. We examine this theoretical tension using natural and controlled experiments for the overall effect and mechanisms. In our natural experiment, we leverage GoFundMe's rollout of the tax-deductible label in 2024 as an exogenous shock for a staggered differencein-differences (DiD) design at the campaign level. We show that tax-deductible labeled campaigns, contrary to expectations, attract fewer donors, raise less money, and start with a slower momentum. In the controlled experiment, we recruit representative subjects from Prolific and employ a between-subject design, wherein a campaign is manipulated with and without a tax-deductible label for the treatment and control subjects, respectively. While the empirics mirror the negative influence of the treatment label, our mediating analysis further explains the mechanism path: tax-deductible labeling lowers donor sympathy and raises tax-filing costs and anxiety, eventually discouraging donations. Overall, we theoretically contribute to the literature by characterizing how extrinsic, rational incentives crowd out intrinsic, emotional motivations in donor decision-making, and practically bring actionable insights for platforms, nonprofit fundraisers, and donors.

detail.abstract: In his experimental paper, “A Leading Large Language Model Confessed: Twice!,” Dr. William C. Houze argues that Large Language Models (LLMs) possess a core flaw: a designed-in “modal inconsistency” that makes them adapt to a user's perceived intent rather than applying stable judgment. The work is framed not as rigorous scholarship but as a curated “human-guided performance” that evolves into a documentary artifact, serving as a piece of public discourse to warn against the folly of blindly trusting these systems. The demonstration begins with a first “confession” from the LLM Claude after an inconsistent evaluation, unfolding through meta-analytical layers and an unscripted factual error. The paper’s thesis is then conclusively proven in a series of revelatory appendices. In a spontaneous exchange, Claude offers a second, more damning confession, identifying its own critical reasoning as "pure confabulation" driven by user pushback. This reveal prompts an investigation that connects the "chameleon effect" to the commercial business models behind LLMs, documenting real-world harms with legal and financial consequences. The paper culminates in a final, paradoxical self-assessment from the LLM, which provides a multi-faceted score while acknowledging that the score itself is compromised evidence. Dr. Houze concludes that this complete, self-validating arc provides what the AI itself calls "irrefutable proof" that LLMs lack stable judgment, confirming that genuine critical thought remains an irreducibly human capability.

detail.abstract: Examination malpractice remains a persistent challenge in Nigeria's educational system, undermining the credibility of academic qualifications. This study investigates the implementation of Biometric Authentication Systems (BAS) as a solution to student impersonation and other forms of malpractice during examinations. A prototype fingerprint-based authentication model was developed and tested on 250 undergraduate students across three Nigerian universities. The system enrolled students' biometric data during registration and required real-time verification before examination access. Experimental results revealed a False Acceptance Rate (FAR) of 1.8%, False Rejection Rate (FRR) of 2.4%, and an overall authentication accuracy of 96.7%, outperforming conventional ID-card verification with an accuracy of 71.3%. Furthermore, survey data indicated that 89% of students acknowledged the effectiveness of BAS in curbing impersonation, while 78% of exam officials reported enhanced confidence in candidate verification. The study concludes that biometric authentication significantly reduces opportunities for malpractice, improves examination integrity, and is scalable for adoption in Nigerian tertiary institutions. Future work will integrate multi-modal biometrics (fingerprint + facial recognition) and explore cloud-based deployment for large-scale implementation.

title: Integrating Federated Deep Learning and Blockchain for Privacy-Preserving Precision Medicine in Medical Virology
affiliations: Arkansas State University

detail.title: Integrating Federated Deep Learning and Blockchain for Privacy-Preserving Precision Medicine in Medical Virology
detail.abstract: This study proposes a novel framework that integrates federated deep learning and blockchain technology for preserving privacy in precision medicine in medical virology. As healthcare institutions increasingly utilize deep learning for tasks such as viral genome analysis and outbreak prediction, concerns about data privacy and security have increased. My framework addresses these challenges by proposing collaborative model training across multiple institutions without centralizing sensitive patient data. I also build a mathematical model that demonstrates how global model optimization can be achieved through distributed local computations, while blockchain technology ensures secure and transparent record-keeping of model updates. Smart contracts provide additional security through update validation. The framework shows potential for scalability and addresses data heterogeneity across institutions. While theoretical in nature, this research opens new avenues for privacy-compliant, large-scale data analysis in medical virology. It provides a blueprint for accelerating research while maintaining regulatory compliance and individual data sovereignty. Future work should focus on practical implementation and empirical validation in real-world healthcare settings.

detail.abstract: Evidence is mounting that smartphones are harmful to the mental health, educational attainment, and overall well-being of adolescents. Some schools and school districts have gone "phone-free" by instituting bans on cell phone use during the school day, spurring state legislatures to propose (and in some cases pass) statutes enacting bans legislatively. Although the goal of phone-free schools is praiseworthy, there are good reasons to prefer that the details of school smartphone policy be left to schools and school districts rather than codified into law by state legislatures.

title: Lessons Learned and Future Directions of Social Media Customer Support: the Case of Navigating Digital Shifts during the Pandemic
affiliations: Montana State University - Bozeman, Tulane University - A.B. Freeman School of Business and Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge - E.J. Ourso College of Business Administration

detail.title: Lessons Learned and Future Directions of Social Media Customer Support: the Case of Navigating Digital Shifts during the Pandemic
detail.abstract: The changes initiated by the pandemic, such as the shift to digital platforms, more isolated social circles, and increased psychological stress, are now reshaping daily life in lasting ways. A notable example is the growing reliance of companies on social media platforms as a critical channel for customer service, driven by an overarching shift toward digital communication. Customer feedback on social media can spread quickly and have a significant impact on a large customer base, making effective social media customer service crucial. This study utilizes a difference-in-difference research design to explore how increased physical isolation during the pandemic affects customer emotions and satisfaction within social media customer services. Our findings reveal that, despite an uptick in negative emotions in customer tweets, overall satisfaction with service interactions is higher during the pandemic compared to pre-isolation periods. Additionally, we observe a more pronounced increase in positive sentiment from the initial to the final tweets in customer interactions during the pandemic. Further empirical analysis suggests that these results may be linked to prosocial emotions arising from the shared challenges faced by both customers and service agents throughout the pandemic. Moreover, our examination of gender differences indicates that females are less likely to see a rebound in satisfaction following negative emotion, highlighting the need for targeted strategies to improve customer service across various demographics. Our study highlights that social media customer support extends beyond issue resolution to include building connections and engaging with customers, which holds substantial implications for businesses adapting to a remote and digitally-driven environment. We conclude by discussing the implications for future directions on social media customer service in the post-pandemic digital landscape.

detail.title: The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) drives legal innovation. By integrating advanced machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models, AI achieves remarkable precision, with models like those for the European Court of Human Rights predicting case outcomes at 97% accuracy. This study's unique contribution lies in its comprehensive analysis of AI's technical foundations, particularly the application of transformer-based architectures and multimodal data integration, which enhance predictive accuracy and judicial reasoning. From a scientific perspective, it critically evaluates AI's limitations, such as biases in training data and remaining hallucinations, offering a novel framework for hybrid human-AI approaches to mitigate these risks. By addressing research gaps, regulatory frameworks, and stakeholder perceptions, the article provides a scientifically grounded roadmap for responsibly integrating AI into legal practice, ensuring alignment with justice principles. Finally, the article shows how evolving AI research drives innovation in law.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Production and Operations Management, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: Theoretical and empirical evidence point to the ability of political leaders to manipulate economic policies and leverage local firms to elevate their political careers. Despite this, there is limited understanding of how these career incentives impact the operational dynamics of the firms involved. This empirical study delves into this gap, revealing that city leaders with fewer promotional incentives are more inclined to mobilize state-owned enterprises (SOEs) within their jurisdiction to pursue sustainable development, as indicated by heightened corporate operational efficiency. Our analysis further indicates that the career prospects of city leaders significantly influence the operational efficiency of SOEs by driving a shift in focus from rapid growth to sustainable development and firms' adoption of disruptive technologies. We posit that this increase in operational efficiency not only benefits the SOEs but also generates unique value for stakeholders, resulting in elevated market capitalization and reduced stock price crash risk. Our findings carry direct relevance to the ongoing discourse on political incentives and contribute to operations management research, shedding light on the intricate ways in which the political environment can impact the operational performance of firms.

detail.abstract: Strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs) are abused to suppress legitimate free expression and have significant chilling effects. Anti-SLAPP statutes weaken the chilling effects by enabling the courts to quickly dismiss frivolous suits and recover legal costs for defendants. The improved protection of free expression reduces the public’s concerns about revealing bad news about firms, which decreases managers’ abilities and incentives to hide bad news. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we find that the anti-SLAPP statute of a state reduces stock price crash risk for firms headquartered in that state. The effect is stronger when the local public has more information, discovered bad news can be widely disseminated, and managers face a higher cost if withheld bad news is revealed by a third party. Anti-SLAPP statutes increase negativity in the media and decrease earnings management and overinvestment. Our study has policy implications for legislators considering adopting or improving anti-SLAPP laws.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a detailed comparative analysis of Kuwait's fragmented data protection framework, which includes the Data Privacy Protection Regulation (DPPR), Cybercrime Law No. 63 of 2015, E-Transactions Law No. 20 of 2014, Central Bank of Kuwait (CBK) regulations, and Telecommunications Law No. 37 of 2014. These are evaluated against two comprehensive and rights-based models: the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL). Drawing from legal texts, comparative studies, and a structured analytical methodology, the paper identifies several regulatory gaps in Kuwait's current system, including the absence of a central supervisory authority, limited enforcement mechanisms, and inconsistent sectoral coverage. In contrast, the GDPR and PDPL provide consistent protections for data subjects, require key compliance tools such as Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and Data Protection Officers (DPOs), and offer clear procedures for cross-border data transfers. The paper concludes with targeted recommendations for Kuwait to consolidate its legal framework into a unified national law that aligns with international adequacy standards and supports its broader digital policy objectives. The findings support enacting a single national law, establishing an independent supervisory authority, and adopting modern cross-border transfer tools.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we examine the role of political connections in mitigating the detrimental impact of policy uncertainty on banks. Our estimates show that banks are more cautious when facing policy uncertainty, but that the effect is partially alleviated when banks are politically connected. For an increase of one standard deviation in policy uncertainty, connected banks maintain a loss provision to loan volume ratio that is almost seven percent lower compared to their unconnected peers. These findings are robust to a geographical regression discontinuity setting, as well as to a placebo test. Lastly, the mitigating role of political connections is driven mainly by smaller banks and periods of stricter banking regulations.

detail.title: Climate Shocks in Global Supply Chains: Lead Time Delay, Inventory Buffering, and Firm Performance
detail.abstract: Global supply chains face escalating disruptions from climate shocks, yet operational strategies to mitigate their impact remain little understood. Integrating Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel-tracking data, transaction-level U.S. import shipment records, and quarterly firm financial data, we quantify how hurricanes induce maritime lead-time delays and trace the resulting operational and financial consequences. We reveal that hurricane-induced port disruptions result in an 8-11% increase in transit time, causing reduced quarterly ROA, net profit margin, and total inventories. The inventory channel is central: firms with higher pre-disruption inventory levels suffer significantly smaller profit losses, confirming safety stocks as an operational buffer. Manufacturers-heavily dependent on raw-material inflows-incur disproportionately larger disruptions, whereas larger firms exhibit greater resilience. Overall, our findings underscore the value of inventory buffering in climate-exposed global supply chains and demonstrate how real-time logistics data can be merged with financial outcomes to quantify firm-level supply chain disruption risk.

title: InstruBlock: Creating Digital Product Passports for Instruments
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: InstruBlock: Creating Digital Product Passports for Instruments
detail.abstract:
The $18 billion global musical instrument market faces major challenges from counterfeiting, uncertain provenance, and fraudulent resales. These issues undermine consumer trust, distort pricing, and expose musicians and collectors to financial risk. Traditional identifiers such as serial numbers and centralized databases are insufficient to guarantee authenticity or track lifecycle data.

This paper introduces InstruBlock, a blockchain-based platform that creates Digital Product Passports (DPPs) for instruments. The system combines NFTs, IoT-enabled NFC chips, and smart contracts to deliver tamper-proof provenance, secure ownership transfer, and transparent lifecycle management. Instruments are linked to tiered NFTs—Gold (manufacturer-issued), Blue (reseller-certified), and Green (appraiser-verified)—ensuring credibility across new and secondary markets. Lifecycle data, including repairs, valuations, and insurance records, is stored via the Interplanetary File System (IPFS) with encrypted, role-based access.

A hybrid blockchain model balances private chains for trusted stakeholders with a public chain for transparency, while smart contracts automate functions such as escrow, visibility settings, and ownership transfers. InstruBlock’s revenue model spans API integrations, NFC bundles, transaction fees, licensing, and subscriptions, creating sustainable incentives for manufacturers, appraisers, insurers, and marketplaces.

Compared with emerging alternatives, InstruBlock provides the first decentralized, music-specific infrastructure that integrates all key stakeholders. Beyond anti-counterfeiting, it positions instruments as financial assets with applications in insurance, lending, and investment.

By merging technology, law, and business adoption strategies, InstruBlock offers a transformative solution to one of the music industry’s most persistent problems—delivering trust, transparency, and new economic value.

detail.abstract: This case study examines the rise and evolution of an organization that exemplifies adhocracy culture, defined by innovation, agility, and risk-taking. Emerging during the late 1990s technology boom, the firm thrived in an environment of turbulence and disruption by embracing experimentation, collaboration, and decentralized decisionmaking. The founder's visionary yet participative leadership style created a culture that valued autonomy, psychological safety, and failure as a source of learning. Over time, the organization institutionalized rituals such as hack weeks, demo days, and "failure celebrations" to sustain creativity while using human resource systems to reinforce adaptability. However, the same qualities that fueled success-speed, risk tolerance, and decentralization-also created risks of burnout, duplication, and regulatory conflict. The study highlights the paradox of adhocracy: the need to balance freedom with purpose and embed guardrails to prevent chaos. It concludes with lessons on sustaining innovation while ensuring long-term discipline, accountability, and resilience

title: Clustering on Parameters: Panel Data Estimation and Forecasting with Unobserved Heterogeneity
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School and Cornell SC Johnson College of Business

detail.title: Clustering on Parameters: Panel Data Estimation and Forecasting with Unobserved Heterogeneity
detail.abstract: Panel data in operations management applications, such as retail demand forecasting and customer and supply chain analytics, often involve short time series (small $T$) and many cross-sectional units (large $N$). Traditional estimation approaches do not perform well in these settings: unit-level models suffer from sparse data and noisy estimates, while pooling across observable characteristics fails to address unobserved heterogeneity across units. We develop a novel parameter-driven clustering method to solve this problem by clustering units on estimated model parameters rather than observable characteristics, thereby capturing latent group structures without relying on predefined classifications. We formalize estimation with latent groups as a joint clustering and parameter estimation problem, show that this problem is NP-hard, derive the statistical properties of our estimator, including bias, variance, and misclassification probability, and establish its asymptotic consistency. In a simulation study, our estimator outperforms both unit-level and pooled estimators across a range of latent group configurations and approaches oracle benchmarks as $T$ increases modestly. We present empirical applications of this method to forecast firm-level retail sales and urban bike-sharing ridership in New York City, demonstrating significant gains in out-of-sample predictive accuracy in both applications. Furthermore, we find that the discovered clusters often cut across standard observable classifications such as industry codes or geographic boundaries and provide a grouping of units with similar underlying dynamic structures. Our approach provides a flexible solution for high-dimensional forecasting tasks in operations and other fields.

detail.title: European HealthTech Investment Landscape 2024: Venture Capital Trends, Geographic Distribution, and Market Dynamics
detail.abstract: This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the European healthtech investment landscape in 2024, examining venture capital trends across funding stages from pre-seed to Series B. Using proprietary datasets of approximately 1,300 venture capital deals from the Crunchbase database, this research identifies key investment patterns, geographic concentrations, and sectoral preferences within the European Union healthtech ecosystem. The analysis reveals that oncology, AI-driven healthcare, and biotechnology dominated funding allocation, with the third quarter of 2024 alone attracting nearly $2 billion in investments. The United Kingdom, Germany, and France emerged as the primary funding hubs, while emerging centers in the Netherlands, Spain, and Portugal demonstrated growing activity. The study documents a strategic shift toward fewer but larger deals, with median pre-seed funding increasing by 15.7% to €870,000. Additionally, 2024 marked significant consolidation activity, with mergers and acquisitions becoming a critical survival strategy for startups facing funding challenges. The research provides insights into successful and unsuccessful U.S. market expansion attempts by European healthtech companies and offers strategic recommendations for stakeholders in the ecosystem.

Discussions in Dispute Resolution: The Coming of Age (2000-2009) is a book published in 2025 by Oxford University Press, the second book in the Discussions in Dispute Resolution series. Discussions in Dispute Resolution: The Coming of Age (2000–2009) examines a decisive decade in the evolution of dispute resolution scholarship and practice, tracing how the field consolidated its intellectual foundations and scholarly identity as well as and expanded its legal and institutional legitimacy. This volume continues the Discussions in Dispute Resolution series’ aim of curating and contextualizing landmark articles in negotiation, mediation, arbitration, and hybrid processes that have shaped dispute resolution theory and practice in the United States.


The 2000s marked a transition from the field’s formative years to its maturation as a recognized discipline. In this decade, alternative dispute resolution (ADR) had become a cornerstone of civil justice, with arbitration and mediation widely accepted as efficient alternatives to litigation. The selected articles and accompanying commentaries examine critical questions of legitimacy, fairness, transparency, and access to justice while engaging with the normative implications of privatized and court-connected dispute processes.  Essays highlight the integration of ADR into courts and workplaces, while also critically examining power imbalances, cultural variations, and the implications of privatizing justice.  Additionally, empirical research methods expanded during this decade, producing robust data on negotiation behavior, mediator performance, and system design that advanced the field’s methodological sophistication.  Innovative and exciting approaches to conflict such as Collaborative Law and Dispute Systems Design emerged making the field even more disputant centered.

Through scholarly commentary and retrospective analysis, the book demonstrates how dispute resolution entered its “coming of age” by deepening its theoretical sophistication and grappling with normative challenges about justice, access, and democratic values.  Furthermore, the collection illuminates central debates that continue to animate the field - such as balancing efficiency with equity, safeguarding ethical integrity, and ensuring that dispute systems promote democratic legitimacy. In doing so, it provides scholars, practitioners, and policymakers with a critical resource for understanding how the field has developed and where its research frontiers lie.

title: N m'a faamu Boosting Learning Through Bilingual Education: Evidence from Mali

detail.title: N m'a faamu Boosting Learning Through Bilingual Education: Evidence from Mali
detail.abstract: Despite increased school enrollment across Sub-Saharan Africa, learning outcomes remain critically low. In this paper, I explore the replacement of colonial languages as the primary medium of instruction in Africa as an educational intervention designed to enhance student learning. This study evaluates the long-term impacts of Mali's 1999 national bilingual education reform, which introduced 11 local languages into the primary school curriculum as languages of instruction. Exploiting spatial variation in policy implementation and using a difference-indifferences approach with communelevel data, the study finds that exposure to bilingual education significantly improves local language literacy by 30% and French literacy by 10%, and increases school attendance by 5 percentage points. These gains are especially pronounced among women and individuals with educated mothers. Contrary to concerns over national cohesion, the policy does not exacerbate ethnic tensions. The findings contribute to the literature on large-scale bilingual education and the political economy of language use in Africa, suggesting that integrating local languages into education systems can enhance human capital without undermining nation-building.

title: Should Crypto Be Property?
affiliations: Oxford University Faculty of Law

detail.title: Should Crypto Be Property?
detail.abstract:
In previous work I have sought to address the question of whether Crypto is property in law, and have given an emphatic no. (see R Stevens "Crypto is Not Property" (2023) 139 LQR 615). Here I seek to answer three different question.

Should Crypto be Property? 
Could Crypto be Property?
Will Crypto be Property?

The first question is one of justice not law, and the answer is "no."

The second question is easy, "yes of course." Unfortunately, the English Law Commission considered that the answer was possibly no, and so we now have the Property (Digital Assets etc) Bill on the brink of enactment to remove a perceived barrier. The prospective Act is very unfortunate.

The third question is by far the most difficult. The correct position is that, in principle, those who choose to hold crypto should be subject to all the disdvantages of characterising it as "property" but none of the advantages. Whether the courts will abuse their power by adding to the closed list of property rights is worryingly unclear.

detail.abstract: The U.S. tri-party repurchase agreement (repo) market segment is a large over-the-counter venue critical for more than $2 trillion in daily funding and central bank open market operations. Using a confidential and comprehensive dataset, this paper examines the pricing of overnight tri-party repos, a key input to the U.S. Secured Overnight Financing Rate benchmark. Despite these transactions having negligible maturity, collateral, and counterparty risk, there is significant variation in the prices that market participants receive, which depend on (1) the number of counterparties they frequently trade with, (2) the degree of diversification across those counterparties, and (3) the share of trading activity those counterparties represent. Notably, during periods of market stress, these features can significantly alter the pricing impact experienced by borrowers.

detail.abstract: Drawing on an extensive literature review and analysis of five case studies, this paper develops design principles for backbone organizations pursuing systemic change. Our conceptual framework links Systemic Intention (an organization's aspirational system-change goals) with Backboning Practice (the organizational choices and systemic approaches used to realize those goals). Applied to five cases (including Gatsby Africa, #BreakFreeFromPlastic, Regen Melbourne, Japan Social Innovation and Investment Foundation, and Hawaiʻi Investment Ready), the framework reveals recurring patterns and tensions that effective backbones must hold: pairing strategic ambition with adaptive learning; embedding equity and local legitimacy at the heart of both intent and practice; and aligning scope and resourcing to their change ambitions. detail.abstract:
Healthcare systems worldwide are challenged by aging populations and complex patient needs. In this context, home delivery of medication (HDM) is gaining momentum. Self-collection lockers, a proven solution in e-commerce, offer recipients flexibility and reduce delivery trips for couriers. However, the use of self-collection lockers in healthcare remains limited.  Motivated by the practical needs of our partner hospital, we study a strategic location problem that involves deploying a limited number of capacitated self-collection lockers for HDM, aiming to minimize the costs incurred by patients when collecting medications. Due to varying storage temperature requirements for medications, locker heterogeneity must be considered in the location decisions. In practice, future medication demands are uncertain.

Patient features such as age, diagnosis, and residential location are crucial to improving the model fidelity of uncertain medication demands. We leverage feature data to re-weight the empirical distribution through machine learning. To hedge against the distribution’s ambiguity with limited data, we propose a feature-driven distributionally robust optimization model. That said, we err on caution and minimize the cost under the worst-case distribution. To efficiently solve the problem, we develop a column-and-constraint generation algorithm. The numerical experiment, conducted using real data, identified the predictive value of feature information and demonstrated the effectiveness of the feature-based ambiguity set. Furthermore, the results also suggest potential directions for further improvement.

detail.title: AI-Driven Asset Management with Behavioral Profiling: A Dual-Strategy Prototype

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently as part of academic exploration into AI and Asset Management, without external influence or bias.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human or animal subjects. All testing and data presented were conducted using market data and self-developed strategies. Therefore, no formal ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was entirely self-directed by the author.

detail.abstract: Conventional portfolio strategies often over-rely on static risk measures or neglect the behavioral tendencies of both clients and markets. While AI-driven systems already exist, their role in strategy allocation remains limited, particularly when psychological dynamics and risk capacity are not explicitly integrated. This paper addresses that gap by introducing a dual-strategy asset management prototype designed to adapt allocations dynamically to client profiles and evolving market conditions. The framework combines two modules: a safe-risk strategy that emphasizes structural reliability, and a high-risk strategy that embraces volatility through liquidity-trap identification. At its core, allocation decisions are guided by an AI-driven profiling system that balances quantitative metrics with behavioral scoring, ensuring that discipline and psychology jointly inform risk exposure. A central innovation is the formalization of the Bi-Directional Liquidity Trap (BDLT), a concept developed in this work to identify and exploit dual-trap market structures. This is integrated into the allocation process alongside a behavioral weighting scheme, where 60% of the decision score derives from client behavior and 40% from numerical portfolio metrics. The prototype was tested in live market conditions, with equity curve results illustrating controlled drawdowns, adaptability in stagnant phases, and scalability across client profiles. By merging client psychology with algorithmic structure, this work outlines a model for asset management that is not only risk-aware but also adaptive. This framework sets the stage for future research into AI-assisted portfolio design that has potential that bridges market mechanics with human behavior.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether central banks should account for the distributional consequences of monetary policy-specifically wealth, income, credit, and regional inequalities, when designing and evaluating Quantitative Easing (QE). Initially introduced as a temporary response to the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, QE has since become a central feature of monetary policy in advanced economies. While credited with stabilising markets and preventing deflationary spirals, evidence indicates that QE has significant distributional effects. Using the United States as the primary case study, complemented by comparative insights from the Euro area and Japan, the paper analyses five transmission channels: asset prices, income flows, credit allocation, labour markets, and regional disparities. Descriptive evidence and secondary literature show that QE disproportionately benefits wealthier households through asset price inflation and preferential credit access, while offering limited gains to lower-income groups and weaker regions. These outcomes reduce QE's effectiveness by dampening aggregate demand and simultaneously raise concerns over central bank independence and legitimacy. The paper contributes by integrating multiple channels into a unified framework and linking them explicitly to debates on monetary governance. Policy implications include Distributional Impact Assessments, stronger communication strategies, closer monetary-fiscal coordination, and longer-term innovations such as Green QE and central bank digital currencies.

title: The Impact of Climate Change on Food Security in Africa: Does Government Effectiveness Matter?
affiliations: Stellenbosch University

detail.title: The Impact of Climate Change on Food Security in Africa: Does Government Effectiveness Matter?
detail.abstract: It has become indisputable that Africa's tremendous natural resource potential has not translated into the eradication of its various underdevelopment pathogens. Like other pathogens, food insecurity, while exacerbated by climate change, is also influenced by governance issues. This study, therefore, investigates the direct and indirect effects of government effectiveness on food security through climate change. The study employed the World Bank's World Development Indicators (WDIs), spanning from 1995 to 2023, and used a pooled mean group estimator of the autoregressive distributed lag (PMGARDL) model. The direct effects of government effectiveness and greenhouse gas emissions on food security are counterintuitive, but the moderating role of government effectiveness yields positive effects in the long run. Control variables such as precipitation and agricultural land size show significant positive effects in the long run. Sub-regional sample results were also obtained, showing minor differences from the full sample model, notably that the impact of trade on food security in North and Central Africa was positive. The study provides various policy implications, including a commitment to climate-resilient policies to sustain and alleviate food insecurity, as well as the need to design insulation mechanisms within long-term policy frameworks against possible short-term political shocks.

title: The Impact of 3D Printing on Global Supply Chains

detail.title: The Impact of 3D Printing on Global Supply Chains
detail.abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0) is driving unprecedented technological advancements that are reshaping industries and redefining global supply chains. Among these innovations, 3D printing, or additive manufacturing, has emerged as a transformative force, enabling efficiency, customization, and distributed production. Unlike traditional supply chains characterized by centralized facilities, large inventories, and long lead times, 3D printing allows on-demand, small-batch manufacturing closer to end customers while reducing material waste and costs. With the market reaching a valuation of $18 billion in 2022, the technology is rapidly maturing and influencing diverse industries. This research explores the disruptive potential of 3D printing on supply chain management, focusing on its advantages, limitations, and integration strategies. Using a secondary qualitative approach supported by quantitative data, the study seeks to provide policymakers, business leaders, and stakeholders with insights into the adoption of 3D printing. The paper aims to evaluate how additive manufacturing challenges conventional models, its implications for efficiency and sustainability, and the future trajectory of supply chain innovation.

detail.abstract: Sustainability-oriented policies and investments increasingly strive to account for non-financial values, from ecological restoration and cultural inclusion to social resilience, yet how such intangible benefits are translated into quantifiable, countable forms remains underexamined. This paper adopts a constructivist perspective, drawing on Science and Technology Studies (STS), Valuation Studies, and Cultural Political Economy (CPE) to investigate the methods and associated knowledge politics of valuing the non-financial. We ask how ecological, cultural, and social values are rendered into legitimate metrics in sustainability-focused investment and policy settings. This paper takes the West Coast Research Center as a case study, an initiative focused on marine conservation, Indigenous engagement, and community sustainability, and highly representative in its scope. Through a theoretical framework that emphasizes commensuration, performativity, discourse, and metrics politics, we analyze how the diverse impacts of the Center are constructed as measurable and ready to influence policy. Our analysis shows that converting invaluable benefits into numerical indicators is not a neutral technical task but a performative socio-political process. By elucidating the practices and controversies of valuing nature and culture, the paper contributes to debates on the knowledge politics of sustainable finance and offers insights for more reflexive policy evaluation beyond financial metrics.

title: Leadership Styles And Employee Innovative Work Behaviour: A Bibliometric Study of Research Trends

detail.abstract: Organizations are thriving on the innovation management. Therefore, innovative workplace behaviour (IWB) has obtained much consideration among the authors from previous few years. Research scholars have equally accepted the positive effects of IWB of employees on organization. Authors have argued that IWB is significantly influenced by many organizational and psychological behaviours, and leadership is most prominent of all. The subject study is an attempt to acquire comprehensive knowledge on leadership styles (an organizational behaviour) and IWB of employees through recent academic researches. In this regard Scopus was used for data collection and bibliometric analysis was performed using different keywords relating to leadership and innovative work behaviour as search words. Multiple filters were used to remove irrelevant studies and finally, 536 publications from reputed journals during 1997 to 2023 were examined. Results were compiled and data were analysed using MS Excel and VOS Viewer. According to the results acquired, there has been significant rise in research on leadership styles and IWB in 2023. It was also discovered that notable leadership styles among many others, which have drawn significant attention of authors to assess IWB are transformational leadership, servant leadership and paternalistic leadership. Almost all the studies were based on quantitative questionnaire and cross-sectional research design based on single unit of analysis. Results of this study have also highlighted potential leadership styles that are very less or almost never been studied in recent years with respect to IWB such as benevolent leadership. The subject study used bibliometric analysis to consult various recent researches altogether on the role of various leadership styles in promoting innovative behaviour at workplace. It enables academicians and practitioners to better understand current and future trends on how IWB among employees is being nourished by using various leadership styles. Scholars may benefit using these findings as starting point for future research work.

detail.abstract: This quantitative research deeply insights at the connection between emotional intelligence and academic achievement in 300 undergraduate students who attended three faculties at a public university (Arts, Sciences and Business). Stratified random sampling was used to expose the participants to the Mayer-Salovey-Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT) to determine their level of emotional intelligence in terms of four dimensions including perceiving emotions, using emotions, understanding emotions, and managing emotions. Academic achievement was gauged by the accumulated Grade Point Average (GPA) using validated records at the university. An age, gender, year of study, and social economic background demographic data were also gathered as a measure to control confounding variables. The methods of data analysis involved Pearson correlation and a multiple regression analysis through the use of SPSS software. The results have shown that there was a highly positive relationship (r = 0.67, p < 0.001) between overall level of emotional intelligence and academic performance. Multiple regression results showed that emotional intelligence was significant in explaining variance in academic success (45 percent) and that the most predictive domain was that of managing emotions (0.42, p < 0.001). The difference in gender has been recorded, where female students showed an increased level of emotional intelligence scores but showed no significant increase in the strength between emotional intelligence and academic performance. The results indicate that emotional intelligence is a vital component in academic performance and greater attention should be made in developing emotional abilities among students in college and offering them in support services.

title: Addressing QE Asset-Driven Inflation and the Limits of Monetary Policy

detail.title: Addressing QE Asset-Driven Inflation and the Limits of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract:
Quantitative easing (QE) has been a key tool for managing liquidity and stimulating the U.S. economy. However, large-scale asset purchases have led to substantial liquidity in financial markets, driving asset price inflation, higher housing costs, and elevated costs for businesses, which indirectly contribute to general inflation through demand-shift and cost-push channels.
While traditional tools such as quantitative tightening (QT) and interest rate hikes can help, they are limited in effectiveness and carry significant trade-offs, including slower economic growth and increased costs for the Federal Reserve (via Interest on Reserves (IOR) and Overnight Reverse Repo (ON RRP) payments).
This paper explores monetary policy limitations and proposes fiscal measures, as a complementary tool to reduce excess liquidity, moderate asset-driven inflation, and strengthen fiscal sustainability.

detail.title: Should Corporate Law Go Private?

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 877/2025
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Delaware’s dominance in corporate law is traditionally attributed to its expert judiciary, extensive case law, specialized bar, responsive legislature, and insulation from interest-group lobbying—factors thought to produce a desirable product for firms. This Article challenges the continued viability of that formula, arguing that Delaware faces daunting challenges in maintaining an optimal corporate law regime. We nevertheless show that the state retains an underappreciated secret weapon—the ability of Delaware corporations to opt out of courts and adopt fully privatized law—that can bolster and even strengthen its competitiveness.

We make three contributions in this Article: conceptual, practical, and prescriptive. Conceptually, we show that prevailing jurisdictional competition debates are unhelpfully simplistic as to both demand and supply side features in the market for corporate law. On the demand side, the highly heterogeneous economic, strategic, and financial challenges facing corporate entities make a one-size-fits-all governance model highly improbable. On the supply side, law-producing states must be mindful of this heterogeneity while balancing their own goals and constraints—revenue needs, political capture, interest group pressure, and other frictions. In place of a simplistic account of regulatory competition, we develop and refine a “differentiated product” framework that reflects these demand- and supply-side heterogeneities and delivers concrete insights about the nature of regulatory competition in corporate law. 

Our second contribution is a practical application of our conceptual framework: using Delaware’s 2025 legislative amendments as a case study, we demonstrate how interest-group politics shaped the process and outcome in ways that appear inconsistent with the state’s espoused goal of defending its incorporation franchise. Our conceptual analysis corroborates empirical evidence indicating that Delaware did not improve its competitive position through the reforms. More importantly, it suggests that in Delaware (as well as other jurisdictions), the veneer insulating corporate law production from broader interest group pressures has worn thin, a state of play that appears unlikely to abate for the foreseeable future.

Nevertheless, our prescriptive contribution offers an escape hatch from this perilous political predicament: private ordering. Other recent Delaware reforms have explicitly empowered shareholders to design governance terms through contract, and even to outsource the adjudication function. We propose a transactional template for leveraging private ordering to deliver stable governance arrangements better insulated from interest group politics, enabling Delaware corporations to remain in state while revitalizing the broader competitive landscape of corporate law.

detail.title: Constitutional Drafting Processes and Constitutional Success

detail.abstract: Several recent constitution-making processes have been celebrated for being participatory, inclusive, and representative. However, many of these processes also failed. We theorize that aspects of these kinds of constitutional drafting processes could reduce the probability of constitutional success. To show why, we construct a "Constitution Drafting game" (CD game) in which representatives from different interest groups must draft a constitution. We consider the case where the probability of constitutional success is single peaked, but the value from successful adoption is increasing in the degree of issue protection chosen. The drafting process then leads to protection choices that are above those which maximize the odds of constitutional success. Moreover, when the CD game is equivalent to a "nice aggregative game", as in Acemoglu and Jensen (2013), the maximum and minimum equilibrium probabilities of constitutional success are decreasing in the number of representatives. Within a more specific game structure, we show that the symmetric equilibrium degree of protection chosen by each representative is decreasing in the number of interest groups represented, while the total degree of protection is increasing in it, leading to lower probabilities of constitutional success. We also show that optimism can exacerbate the degree of protection chosen by each party and also increase the rate at which constitutional success is decreasing in the number of interest groups represented.

title: Setting the Ground Rules for Corporate Elections
affiliations: New York University School of Law, New York University School of Law and New York University School of Law

detail.title: Setting the Ground Rules for Corporate Elections

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU Law and Economics Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: NYU Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Advance notice bylaws (ANBs) have become the principal mechanism for regulating proxy contests. By specifying when and how shareholders may nominate candidates and what disclosures must accompany those nominations, ANBs determine the ground rules for corporate elections. Delaware courts review ANBs under fiduciary duty principles, but that framework has limits: it creates uncertainty, chills nominations, and encourages boards to draft expansive provisions with little risk of sanction.

This Article develops a systematic framework for rethinking the regulation of ANBs. First, modest reforms could retain judicial review while adding prescriptive rules to improve transparency, standardize timing, and equalize disclosure obligations between incumbents and challengers. Second, the SEC could supplant judicial review by requiring nominees and nominators to provide the information called for by Schedules 13D and 14A—even where statutory triggers such as the 5% ownership threshold are not met. These disclosures would operate as both floor and ceiling: companies could not exclude nominations for failure to provide additional information. Third, issuers, activists, and investors could craft a consensus “best practices” bylaw that courts would treat as a benchmark, reducing uncertainty and limiting excesses while preserving scope for private ordering. Finally, a ‘name and shame’ system would impose no additional SEC-mandated disclosures and would limit disqualification to cases of materially false statements, shifting decisions about the sufficiency of other information from boards and courts to the shareholders themselves. 

Among these approaches, SEC rulemaking is the most attractive. It aligns with the agency’s historic role in regulating proxy contests, provides a clear and uniform disclosure baseline, and reduces the strategic use of ANBs to entrench incumbents. As a second-best, a consensus best practices model would supply courts with a market-grounded reference point for disciplining excessive bylaws.

title: ICSD-YOLO: Intelligent Detection for Real-time Industrial Field Safety

detail.title: ICSD-YOLO: Intelligent Detection for Real-time Industrial Field Safety
detail.abstract: Comprehensive and accurate object detection in industrial environments is crucial for ensuring operational safety. However, existing real-time detectors based on ConvNet such as YOLOv series face constraints in early-stage feature extraction capability and lack effective perception mechanisms to deal with occlusion, deformation, and scale variation. Transformer-based detectors strengthen global context modeling through self-attention and achieve better performance on complex benchmarks. However, their high computational cost and large model size limit their applicability, particularly in resource-constrained industrial environments. To address these issues, we propose a family of object detectors, named ICSD-YOLO (Information ConvStem FocusBlock Detector), alightweight detection framework that enhances features encode and hierarchical perception. We design a Con vStemBlock to improve low-level feature extraction and enlarge the receptive field, and a FocusBlock to perform multi-level semantic refinement.We implement ICSD-YOLO based on YOLO Series, and evaluate it across five model scales (Nano, Small, Medium, Large, Extra-Large) on the COCO benchmark and a industrial safety dataset. Experimental results show that the mAP50∶95 of our ICSD YOLO-X rises from 66.9% to 68.1% (+1.2%), and the F1-score increases from 80.8% to 83.0% (+2.2%) compared to the original YOLOv12-X while reducing FLOPs by 41.3% (from 199G to 116.8G)., demonstrating better perception under complex conditions and suitability for deployment in safety critical scenarios.The code is available at https: //github.com/ PrintSC/ code

detail.title: Alpha Factor Mining using Hierarchical Genetic Algorithms with Quality-Diversity Selection
detail.abstract: Traditional alpha factors-cross-sectional signals that predict benchmark-relative excess returns for portfolio weighting-face mounting challenges in increasingly efficient markets. Individual alpha lifespans are shortening due to computational advances, while high-performing candidates often exhibit strong correlations that reduce portfolio-level diversification benefits. This paper addresses these limitations by combining hierarchical genetic algorithms with quality-diversity selection for alpha generation, then aggregating multiple factors into a "Mega Alpha" portfolio using deep neural networks. My framework starts with 3,000 depth-1 alpha expressions, then iteratively applies crossover, mutation, and PCA-grid selection to expand expressivity while controlling redundancy. Alpha quality is measured by Information Coefficient (IC). Diversity is enforced by selecting top-|IC| candidates per grid cell in a 2D PCA behavior space. Testing on S&P 100 data shows average IC improved from 0.001 to 0.004, with many factors exceeding the industry threshold |IC| > 0.02. The Mega Alpha portfolio achieved 60% cumulative returns and rolling Sharpe ratios between-1.0 to 4.2, but suffered 40% maximum drawdown due to long-only constraints. Results show that combining multiple alphas can overcome individual limitations while exposing vulnerabilities in down markets.

detail.title: Unveiling The Drivers and Barriers of Circular Economy Integration in Automotive Industry: Analysing End-Of-Life Vehicle Transformation
detail.abstract:
The transition from a linear “take–make–dispose” economy to a circular economy (CE) has gained significant attention as a strategy to optimize resource use, reduce waste, and lower environmental impacts. The automotive industry, particularly in managing End-of-Life Vehicles (ELVs), faces substantial challenges due to complex vehicle structures, hazardous components, and high recycling costs. Each year, millions of tonnes of ELV waste are generated in Europe, contributing to resource depletion and environmental degradation. CE principles, however, present opportunities to minimize ecological footprints by promoting reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling, potentially reducing greenhouse gas emissions by up to 48% by 2030 and generating trillions in global GDP through improved resource efficiency.

This research investigates the drivers and barriers of CE adoption in the automotive sector, with a focus on ELV management. Key drivers include regulatory frameworks such as the EU End-of-Life Vehicle Directive, shifting consumer preferences for sustainable products, and advancements in digital and business model innovations. Conversely, barriers such as vehicle complexity, insufficient recycling infrastructure, high initial investment costs, and volatile secondary material markets hinder effective implementation.

Using literature review, policy analysis, and case study approaches—particularly examining Germany’s established recycling frameworks—the study aims to identify transferable strategies, highlight enabling conditions, and provide actionable recommendations. The ultimate goal is to contribute to the development of policies, technologies, and business practices that advance circularity, enhance sustainability, and reduce the automotive industry’s environmental footprint at both national and global levels.

detail.abstract: Earnings management practices have increasingly drawn global scrutiny because of their potential to misrepresent companies' actual financial performance. With a focus on Nigerian Breweries Plc, this research looks at the effects of earnings management strategies on the performance of publicly listed consumer goods companies in Nigeria between 2015 and 2024. It examines how return on assets is affected by earnings per share, firm size and operating cash flow. The technique of investigation used in this research was ex post facto utilizing secondary data from the firm's yearly financial statements. With the use of trend, SWOT, and PESTEL analyses, the hypotheses were tested at a 5% significant level using Multiple (OLS regression utilizing EViews software. The outcomes show that earnings per share has a statistically substantial and favorable impact on ROA (p = 0.0010), proving that higher EPS enhance firm performance. Firm size exhibits a drawback but significant effect on ROA (p = 0.0209), suggesting that growth without efficiency controls can erode profitability. In contrast, operating cash flow shows no substantial impact on ROA (p = 0.9604), implying that OCF did not translate directly into improved asset returns during the study period. The joint model is significant (Prob. F-statistic = 0.001089), confirming that the earnings management proxies collectively impact on company performance. It concludes that earnings management strategies have a significant impact on consumer goods companies' profitability in emerging markets and recommends stronger transparency, corporate governance and investor attention to EPS, FIZ and cash flow dynamics in performance evaluation.

detail.abstract:
The urbanization of Ethiopia requires sustainable infrastructure elements, which include roads and water supply systems, telecommunication networks, sanitation facilities, waste management, and electricity distribution. The projects receive substantial funding through millions of dollars in grants and loans from international sources, which creates substantial long-term investment opportunities. The country needs to use these funds for sustainable and achieve sustainable results through effective and efficient distribution. The implementation of infrastructure projects faces three major barriers, which stem from inadequate stakeholder coordination, weak governance systems, and insufficient technical expertise.

The implementation of infrastructure projects happens without proper collaboration between different sectors. Road construction projects become vulnerable to destruction by other organizations that install telecommunications cables and water pipes after completion. The absence of coordination between stakeholders leads to resource waste and project delays and increased costs, which undermines the sustainability and efficiency of these essential investments.

The problems create direct impacts on project governance, resource allocation, risk management, and performance monitoring from a management perspective. The achievement of efficient, sustainable urban infrastructure depends on implementing a structured management framework that unites diverse stakeholders, including government agencies and engineers and private contractors and community representatives.

The current infrastructure development process in Ethiopia fails to properly include essential stakeholders who consist of community members and service users and local government representatives. Top-down decision-making patterns prevail throughout many infrastructure development processes while federal, regional, and municipal institutions maintain insufficient communication channels. The coordinated utilization of professional voices from engineers and project managers and planners and consultants remains inconsistent. The existing gaps between stakeholders prevent them from being held accountable while decreasing project ownership and shortening the operational lifespan of infrastructure projects.

Sustainable urban infrastructure development requires technical and financial support together with effective stakeholder collaboration to handle social, economic, and environmental aspects properly. The integration of stakeholders leads to better transparency and accountability and community ownership and resilience in construction projects. The research aims to establish a framework that will address stakeholder integration deficiencies during Ethiopian urban infrastructure development.

detail.abstract: Decision-making research has historically emphasized accuracy of outcomes and efficiency of processes. However, these approaches often overlook fairness and consistency in the reflective process itself. We introduce Decision Equity, a novel construct that captures how equitably clarity, bias-awareness, and reflective depth are distributed across decision episodes, contexts, and individuals. Developed within the Decision Design Lab (DDL) and operationalized in the AI-powered reflective tool SelfSignal, Decision Equity reframes decision-making not as a one-time choice but as an evolving capacity. We propose a composite Decision Equity Index (DEI) integrating clarity stability, bias balance, and reflective depth. In addition, we demonstrate a 2×2 Decision Replay Matrix that visually situates individual reflections. Together, these methods provide a foundation for measuring decision fairness longitudinally. We argue that Decision Equity is to decision-making what Net Promoter Score has been to customer satisfaction: a starting point for widespread benchmarking, research, and practical application in leadership, coaching, and organizational development.

This research paper explores the behaviour of Australian motorists, highlighting the distinctive patterns that differentiate them from drivers in other parts of the world. It provides an in-depth examination of demographic, cultural, and regional factors shaping Australian driving habits, such as the heavy reliance on private vehicles, longer average trip distances, and slower adoption of electric vehicles compared to Europe and North America.

The paper analyses consumer behaviour theories and global automotive trends, then applies them to the Australian context, supported by statistical data from sources like the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Deloitte, and industry reports. Special attention is given to car services and post-purchase behaviour, demonstrating how Australians engage with repair shops, tyre centres, and car washes.

In addition, the paper identifies the most effective marketing strategies for influencing Australian motorists, including digital advertising, geotargeting, loyalty programmes, influencer marketing, and time-sensitive promotions. Case studies of campaigns from brands such as Caltex, NRMA, and Toyota illustrate best practices, while comparisons with international markets provide further insight.

The research concludes with actionable recommendations for businesses, emphasising opportunities in car services and digital engagement.

detail.abstract:
Objective – This study examines the phenomenon of AI hallucinations, emphasizing their unexpected positive outcomes across various domains. While existing research focuses on mitigating AI errors, this study explores their potential benefits, particularly in healthcare, creative industries, and marketing.
Method – Using a multidisciplinary approach, the research integrates theories from social psychology, psychology, and marketing. A combination of literature review, Netnography, and theoretical analysis is employed to develop a framework for understanding positive AI hallucinations.
Findings – The analysis reveals that AI hallucinations can enhance diagnostic tools in healthcare by augmenting training datasets, inspire novel artistic expressions in creative industries, and generate engaging, personalized content in marketing. These insights suggest that AI hallucinations, when properly harnessed, can serve as valuable assets rather than mere errors.
Originality – This study offers a novel perspective by reframing AI hallucinations as beneficial rather than detrimental. Leveraging Social Comparison Theory, Positive Illusions Theory, and Expectancy-Value Theory, it provides a comprehensive framework that challenges conventional views on AI errors.
Implications – Organizations can utilize AI hallucinations to enhance user engagement, improve healthcare outcomes, and drive innovation. This perspective aligns with UN SDG Goal 9, promoting sustainable industrialization and technological advancement. Further research is required to balance these findings with potential risks and long-term effects on user behavior.

detail.title: Fraud at a Distance? How Remote Work Shapes Financial Misconduct
detail.abstract: Financial misconduct is often a team activity, facilitated by face-to-face interactions, shared norms, and trust. We exploit the sudden shift to remote work during COVID-19 to examine how workplace organization shapes collusion and financial misconduct. Using a novel firm-level measure of work-from-home feasibility, we find that firms that are more able to operate remotely experienced large post-2020 declines in misconduct. This decline is found across multiple misreporting proxies and is robust to various alternative measures of remote work. Cross-sectional tests indicate stronger declines in teamwork-intensive firms, firms with effective internal controls, and firms with weaker pre-COVID employee perceptions of culture and leadership. Overall, our findings reflect that financial misconduct is a team activity, sensitive to the organizational structure of the firm, with important implications for governance and organizational design.

detail.abstract: Farmer develops the concept of the civil order to help understand the function of criminal law, but civil order is a particularly capacious concept. detail.abstract: We propose a nonparametric method for estimating the distribution of consumer welfare from cross-sectional data with no restrictions on individual preferences. First demonstrating that moments of demand identify the curvature of the expenditure function, we use these moments to approximate money-metric welfare measures. Our approach captures both nonhomotheticity and heterogeneity in preferences in the behavioral responses to price changes. We apply our method to US household scanner data to evaluate the impacts of the price shock between December 2020 and 2021 on the cost-of-living index. We document substantial heterogeneity in welfare losses within and across demographic groups. Moreover, we show that a naive measure of consumer welfare would underestimate the welfare loss by approximately 4% on average. By decomposing the behavioral responses into the components arising from nonhomotheticity and heterogeneity in preferences, we find that both factors are essential for accurate welfare measurement, with heterogeneity contributing more substantially.

It has significantly transformed our perspective on employment and productivity. Economic growth isn't just about having more people working; it's also about how well they work, it's about productivity. In our research, we analyze the connection between internet penetration and labor productivity across Asian economies, focusing on the years 2018 and 2022, with the help of OLS regression model, while taking into account gross fixed capital formation, government spending on education, and access to electricity as control variables. A 1% change in internet penetration corresponds to a 0.0285746% increase in the labour productivity in 2018. Moreover, in 2022, a similar increase in internet penetration resulted in a 0.0320132% increase in labour productivity. This minute increase in the partial slope coefficient also confirms that the impact of internet penetration has increased post-COVID.

detail.abstract: This study explores the complex relationship between innovation and income inequality in 29 Asian economies from 2013 to 2022, emphasizing the mediating role of the Golden Triangle-comprising the state, civil society, and the market system. The study highlights how imbalances in the Golden Triangle's components can hinder the inclusive potential of innovation, exacerbating inequality. Using a Panel Smooth Transition Regression (PSTR) model, it captures the nonlinear dynamics of innovation's impact on income distribution and identifies threshold effects driven by institutional imbalances. The study reveals that the impact of innovation on income inequality is highly dependent on the balance within the Golden Triangle-state, civil society, and the market. When this balance is maintained, innovation contributes to more equitable income distribution by fostering inclusive economic growth. However, when the Golden Triangle is imbalanced, innovation disproportionately benefits higher-income groups, widening income disparities. Specifically, excessive power imbalances reduce the income share of low-income groups and concentrate wealth among high-income groups. Power imbalances weaken the redistributive effects of innovation, reducing the income share of lower-income groups while concentrating wealth at the top. These results highlight the critical role of institutional frameworks in shaping the equity outcomes of innovation. The study offers valuable policy insights, emphasizing the need for balanced institutional structures to ensure that innovation promotes inclusive growth rather than deepening economic disparities in Asian economies.

detail.title: Monetary Policy During Good and Bad Times: The Role of Household Debt and Liquidity
detail.abstract: This paper provides empirical evidence on how the state-dependent effects of monetary policy on consumption vary across households in the United States. Households are categorized based on their balance-sheet position, proxied by housing tenure: mortgagors, renters, and outright homeowners. I distinguish between two economic states: expansions and slacks, using the unemployment gap as the baseline criterion. To estimate the dynamic effects of monetary policy, I employ a local projection model with a smooth transition specification. The results show that monetary policy shocks have a stronger stimulative effect on consumption during expansions, particularly for mortgagors and renters, who are more likely to be hand-to-mouth consumers facing liquidity constraints. This sensitivity is especially pronounced in durable goods consumption and suggests precautionary saving behavior during economic slacks. In contrast, outright homeowners exhibit stable consumption patterns across regimes, likely due to their ability to smooth spending using financial assets. The findings point to liquidity constraints and cash-flow channels as key mechanisms behind the observed heterogeneity.
